title: LCA of a Municipal Plastic Waste Recycling System: Collection Routes Compared
sub: A system-level assessment of managing one tonne of household plastic packaging waste, comparing kerbside collection, a deposit-return system, mixed-waste sorting and export.
pdf: Case 09 — LCA of a Municipal Plastic Recycling System: Executive Summary
fu: Management of 1 tonne of household plastic packaging waste collected in a European municipality (mixed PET, HDPE, PP, LDPE film and other plastics)
ref: 1,000 kg of collected plastic packaging waste; outputs of recyclate, sorting and reprocessing residues, and recovered energy
boundary: Gate-to-grave with system expansion: collection, sorting at a material recovery facility (MRF), baling and transport, reprocessing into recyclate, treatment of residues, and credits for avoided virgin polymer and avoided grid energy
geo: Western European municipality; export scenario to South-East Asia
method: EF 3.1 characterisation; IPCC AR6 GWP100; system expansion with substitution factors for recyclate quality
alloc: System expansion (avoided burden): recyclate credited with avoided virgin polymer multiplied by a substitution factor for quality (0.6–0.95); energy recovery credited with avoided grid electricity and heat
cutoff: Flows <1% of mass and energy excluded (wire for baling, MRF consumables) with cumulative exclusions <5%; infrastructure included through database processes
dq: Eurostat waste statistics, published MRF and recycling LCAs, PlasticsEurope eco-profiles; no operator data. Overall data quality Medium; Low for export fate
srcShort: Illustrative model; parameters within ranges from Eurostat, PlasticsEurope eco-profiles, published waste-management LCAs and Plastics Recyclers Europe reports.
loop: Circular loop: recyclate replaces virgin polymer in new products and packaging
exec:
This case study assesses a waste-management system rather than a product: how one tonne of household plastic packaging waste is collected, sorted, recycled or treated. Municipal plastic recycling is a policy priority under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, which sets recycling targets for plastic packaging of 50% by 2025 and 55% by 2030, and under the EU plastic own resource (a levy of €0.80 per kg of non-recycled plastic packaging waste).
The system is modelled with credits for avoided virgin plastic and energy. In the kerbside baseline, the net result is +165 kg CO2e per tonne: recycling 560 kg of recyclate saves more than reprocessing costs, but incinerating 440 kg of sorting and reprocessing residues adds about 1,000 kg CO2e. For comparison, incinerating the whole tonne would emit roughly 1,500 kg CO2e net.
A deposit-return system gives the best result (−988 kg CO2e) because it delivers clean, single-polymer bottles with high yields. Mixed-waste sorting performs worst (+1,084 kg), because quality is low and residues are high. Export results in +683 kg and carries uncertain fate and leakage risks that LCA does not capture well.
Recommendations focus on collection quality, design for recycling and sorting efficiency. For CSRD, results are relevant for waste companies (E1, E2, E5) and for packaging producers reporting end-of-life impacts and recyclability.
overview:
Household plastic packaging is a heterogeneous waste stream: bottles, trays, films and multilayer items made from different polymers, often contaminated with food and labels. How it is collected strongly affects how much becomes high-quality recyclate.
The purpose of this LCA is to compare collection and treatment routes and to show which system parameters (sorting efficiency, recyclate quality, residue treatment) drive the climate result.
goal: The goal is to support municipal waste planning, waste-management company strategy and producer responsibility organisations in choosing collection systems and investments. The audience includes policymakers, waste operators and packaging producers' ESG teams.

stages.what: Kerbside collection of separately collected plastic packaging (or deposit returns, or residual waste).
stages.as: Separate kerbside collection; DRS uses retailer backhaul

stages.what: Near-infrared sorting, ballistic separation, eddy-current and manual quality control into polymer streams.
stages.out: PET, HDPE, PP, film and mixed-plastic bales; sorting residues

stages.what: Bales are transported to reprocessors (or shipped abroad in the export scenario).
stages.tr: 300 km by truck; 9,000 km by ship for export
stages.so: Export to countries with weak waste controls

stages.what: Shredding, washing, flotation, drying, extrusion and pelletising into recyclate.
stages.ew: ≈4,500 MJ and 3,500 L water per tonne input

stages.what: Sorting and reprocessing residues are incinerated with energy recovery.
stages.em: Fossil CO2 (≈2.3 t per t plastic)

stages.what: Credit for virgin polymer production avoided by using recyclate.
Credit for grid electricity and heat displaced by energy recovery.
stages.as: Displaced marginal grid mix, declining over time

lci: Per tonne input, washing and extrusion
≈2.3 kg CO2 per kg mixed plastic

hot.why: Every tonne of plastic burned releases about 2.3 t of fossil CO2. Residues from sorting and reprocessing are the largest burden in all routes.
Low sorting efficiency increases residues and lowers recyclate output; contamination from non-recyclable designs and food residues reduces yields.
Low-quality recyclate replaces less virgin plastic or is downcycled, reducing the credit that makes recycling beneficial.
Washing and extrusion are the main gross burdens of recycling and the main water use.
Shipping adds emissions, and mismanagement abroad creates leakage and open-burning risks not well captured by LCA.

sens.t: Sensitivity: substitution factor of recyclate for virgin plastic
sens.xl: Substitution factor (share of virgin plastic replaced per kg recyclate)
sens.note: Recyclate quality and the treatment of residues are the most influential parameters. The second line shows a counter-intuitive result that needs careful interpretation.
sens.interp: On climate change alone, landfilling plastic residues looks better than incinerating them, because plastic carbon stays in the landfill. This ignores resource loss, land use, leachate risks and the EU Landfill Directive, which limits landfill to 10% of municipal waste by 2035. Single-indicator conclusions can mislead.

wf: Renewable power at MRF and reprocessor

ci.stage: Residue incineration is the largest burden and the avoided virgin polymer the largest credit. The net result depends on the balance between them.
ci.stage_e: Avoided virgin polymer production (feedstock energy) dominates energy results, making the system a net energy saver.
ci.stage_w: Reprocessing uses water, but avoided virgin production saves more, giving a net water benefit.
ci.donut: Of the gross burdens, residue incineration accounts for about 72%: reducing residues is the most effective lever.
ci.sankey: Of each tonne collected, 560 kg become recyclate; 440 kg are incinerated as sorting and reprocessing residues.
ci.heat: Residue treatment is the climate hotspot; reprocessing is the energy and water hotspot.
ci.scen: Deposit-return systems deliver net savings; mixed-waste sorting and export deliver net burdens. Collection quality decides the outcome.
ci.scenNote: Negative values are credits for avoided virgin plastic and grid energy (system expansion).
ci.radar: Semi-quantitative profile: DRS is lowest on every axis; export has the highest leakage and transport scores.
ci.wf: Better sorting and design-for-recycling together can turn the kerbside system from a net burden into a net saving.

interp.m: Recycling plastic is clearly better than incinerating all of it, but the net benefit depends on how much of the collected material becomes high-quality recyclate. Clean collection streams make the biggest difference.
interp.a: Substitution factor; sorting and reprocessing yields; residue treatment route; grid mix for credits; export fate.
interp.u: Substitution factors are uncertain and debated; export fate data are poor; credits depend on the energy mix displaced, which is changing as grids decarbonise.
interp.can: Deposit-return systems and better sorting improve results; residues and low-quality recyclate drive burdens; export carries unquantified risks.
interp.cannot: The study cannot conclude that landfill is preferable (it ignores resource loss and other impacts), or that recycling is always beneficial regardless of quality.
interp.d: Collection system design (DRS adoption), MRF investment, packaging design requirements, export policies and waste-company ESG targets.

recs: Design packaging for existing sorting technology: mono-materials, NIR-detectable colours, washable labels.
Buy recyclate from traceable domestic sources with quality specifications; avoid suppliers relying on export routes.
Use recyclate in closed-loop applications to maximise substitution; share specifications with recyclers.
Support deposit-return systems and in-store collection; avoid hard-to-recycle formats in own-label ranges.
Invest in sorting technology (NIR, AI-assisted), renewable energy and washing water recycling; publish yield and quality data.
Report actual recycling outcomes (not collection) and residues; avoid claiming credits that buyers of recyclate also claim.
Introduce deposit-return systems, eco-modulated EPR fees, quality standards for recyclate, and controls on waste exports.

take: How plastic is collected decides whether recycling delivers a climate benefit: clean deposit-return streams save almost a tonne of CO2e per tonne, while mixed-waste sorting and export add emissions and risks.
biz: Invest in collection quality (deposit-return, better kerbside sorting) and design-for-recycling, report actual recycling outcomes rather than collection, and phase out exports of low-quality mixed plastics.
assume: System expansion with substitution factors 0.6–0.95; incineration 2.3 kg CO2/kg plastic with energy recovery credits; 300 km domestic transport; 30% mismanagement in export scenario (illustrative). Leakage not quantified.
